title: Promoted but Not Measured: The Adequacy of Official Data for Evaluating Festival Tourism in Accra, Ghana
content: Governments across the Global South now promote cultural festivals as tourism assets, but few of them measure what those festivals actually do. This article asks whether the official data that already exist in Ghana are adequate for evaluating the tourism role of two festivals in Accra: Homowo, the harvest festival of the Ga people, and the Chale Wote Street Art Festival, which began in 2011. The study draws on 21 official and statistical sources, 84 months of international arrivals, the 2023 national domestic tourism survey, licensed-enterprise registers, and a corpus of 53 media and official texts. Each source is assessed against five criteria: relevance, resolution, consistency, coverage and access. August arrivals run about 10 per cent above an average month, yet they cannot be distinguished statistically from July (p = 0.50). Domestic culture and festival trips cluster in July to September but make up only about 1 per cent of overnight trips. Thirty-two inconsistencies were logged across sources, among them a change in the basis of 2023 receipts that roughly halves the apparent growth between 2023 and 2024. Four gaps, in resolution, coverage, consistency and attribution, rule out any estimate of festival effects. Yet the national tourism authority already surveys December in GH, Kwahu Easter and PANAFEST. The obstacle, then, is not capacity. It is an asymmetry in which the state promotes festivals it does not measure. The article offers a fitness-for-use framework for festival-tourism data in data-scarce destinations and sets out practical steps for closing the gap.
